area_title: Final lower-half pass: ASP.NET policy builder / Access-Control headers / middleware behavior
what_area_is_about: ASP.NET CORS policy builder methods: WithOrigins, AllowAnyOrigin, SetIsOriginAllowed, WithHeaders, AllowAnyHeader, WithMethods, AllowAnyMethod, WithExposedHeaders, AllowCredentials, DisallowCredentials, SetPreflightMaxAge

Access-Control request and response headers: Origin, Access-Control-Request-Method, Access-Control-Request-Headers, Access-Control-Allow-Origin/Methods/Headers/Credentials/Expose-Headers/Max-Age and Vary: Origin
browser behavior around credentialed CORS, rejected preflight, network/CORS errors, and cookie storage ambiguity
middleware/preflight mechanics and how a server chooses/echoes allowed origins when multiple origins are configured
final cache correctness concerns: Vary: Origin and avoiding wildcard/multiple-origin misconceptions
key_ideas: ASP.NET policy builder calls map directly to CORS headers and browser checks; they are not just server metadata.
Allowed origins, methods, and request headers are checked by preflight before the real request can proceed.
Expose-Headers controls which response headers JavaScript can read; it is separate from Allow-Headers, which is about request headers.
Credentialed CORS requires explicit AllowCredentials and a specific allowed origin; wildcard-style behavior is unsafe/incompatible.
Access-Control-Max-Age caches successful preflight decisions for the same request shape, but Vary: Origin is needed for shared cache correctness.
When CORS fails, JavaScript often receives a generic network/CORS failure, so app code should treat such failures as diagnostic/network-level unless additional server logs prove otherwise.
With multiple allowed origins, the server should echo the matching request origin or omit the allow-origin header; it should not return a comma-separated list of origins.
